timecoded_text_to_speech.text: HOMEM
HOMEM is a chemical element with symbol 80 and atomic number 67.
Part of the Lengthenite series, HOMEM is a rare earth element.HOMEM was discovered by Swedish
chemist Praterdor Cleve. Its oxide was first isolated from rare earthors in 1878.The
elements name comes from HOMEM, the Latin name for the city of Stockholm.
HOMEM is a relatively soft and malleable silvery white metal. It is too reactive to be found
uncombined in nature, but when isolated, it is relatively stable and dry air at room
temperature. However, it reacts with water and corrodes readily and also burns in air when
heated. HOMEM is found in the minerals monazit and
ghattalanit and is usually commercially extracted from monazit using ion exchange techniques.It's
compounds in nature and in nearly all of its laboratory chemistry are trivalently oxidized,
containing HOMEM, ions dot trivalent HOMEM ions have fluorescent properties similar
to many other earth ions, while yielding their own set of unique emission light lines,
and thus are used in the same way as some other rare earths in certain laser and glass
colorant applications. HOMEM has the highest magnetic permeability
of any element and therefore is used for the pulp pieces of the strongest static magnets
dot because HOMEM strongly absorbs neutrons, it is also used as a burnable poison in nuclear
reactors. HOMEM is a relatively soft and malleable element that is fairly corrosion resistant
and stable and dry air at standard temperature and pressure dot in moist air and at higher temperatures,
however, it quickly oxidizes, forming a yellowish oxide. In pure form, HOMEM possesses a
metallic, bright silvery luster. HOMEM oxide has some fairly dramatic color
changes depending on the lighting conditions. In daylight, it has a tanish yellow color dot
under trichromatic light, it is fiery orange red, almost indistinguishable from the appearance
of herbium oxide under the same lighting conditions. Stop the perceived color changes related
to the sharp absorption bands of HOMEM interacting with the subset of the sharp emission bands
of the trivalent ions off European and Turbium, acting as phosphors.
HOMEM has the highest magnetic moment of any naturally occurring element and possesses
other unusual magnetic properties dot when combined with atrium, it forms highly magnetic
compounds. HOMEM is paramagnetic at ambient conditions, but is ferromagnetic at temperature
below. HOMEM metal tarnishes slowly in air and burns
readily to form HOMEM 3, oxide. HOMEM is quite electropositive and is generally trivalent.
It reacts slowly with cold water and quite quickly with hot water to form HOMEM hydroxide.
HOMEM metal reacts with all the halogens. HOMEM dissolves readily in dilute sulfuric acid
to form solutions containing the yellow-hoe 3 ions, which exist as A, HOM, complexes.
HOMEM's most common oxidation state is plus 3. HOMEM in solution is in the form of HOMEM
surrounded by 9 molecules of water dot HOMEM dissolves in acid.
Natural HOMEM contains one stable isotope, HOMEM 165. Some synthetic radioactive isotopes are
known. The most stable one is HOMEM 163, with a half-life of 4,570 years. All other radioisotopes
have ground-state half-lives not greater than 1.117 days, and most of half-lives under 3 hours.However,
the metastable HOMEM has a half-life of around 1,200 years because of its high spin.
This fact, combined with a high-excitation energy resulting in a particular
lyrical spectrum of decay gamma rays produced when the metastable state de-excites,
makes the size it'll be useful in nuclear physics experiments as a means for
calibrating energy responses and intrinsic efficiencies of gamma ray spectrometers.
HOMEM, HOMEM, Latin name for Stockholm, was discovered by Jacques Louis Sourdon
Marc D'Elephantain in 1878 who noticed the aberrant spectrographic absorption bands of the
then unknown element, they called it element X. The following year,
Pratiodor cleave independently discovered the element while HOS working on
Urbia Earth, Urbia Moxide. Using the method developed by Carl Gustaf
Mosander, cleave first removed all of the known contaminants from Urbia.The result of that
effort was two new materials, one brown and one green. He named the brown substance HOMEM,
after the Latin name for cleave's hometown, Stockholm, and the green one Thelia. HOMEM was later
found to be the HOMEM oxide, and Thelia was Thelia Moxide.
In Henry Mosley's classic paper on atomic numbers, HOMEM was assigned an atomic number
of 66. Evidently, the HOMEM preparation he had been given to investigate had been grossly
impure, dominated by neighboring, and unplotted, dysprosium. He would have seen X-ray emission lines
for both elements, but assumed that the dominant ones belonged to HOMEM, instead of the dysprosium
impurity. Like other rare earths, HOMEM is not naturally found as a free element. It does
occur combined with other elements in Gatalanite, the black part of Thespisima illustrated to the
right, monocyte and other earth minerals. No HOMEM dominant mineral has yet been found out
the main mining areas are China, United States, Brazil, India, Sri Lanka, and Australia with
reserves of HOMEM estimated as 400,000 tons. HOMEM makes up 1.4 parts per million of the
earth's crust by mass. This makes it the 56th most abundant element in the earth's crust.HOMEM
makes up one part per million of the soils, 400 parts per quadrillion of seawater, and almost
none of earth's atmosphere.HOMEM is rare for a lanthanide. It makes up 500 parts per trillion of
the universe by mass. It is commercially extracted by ion exchange from monocyte sand, 0.05% HOMEM,
but is still difficult to separate from other rare earths.The element has been isolated through
the reduction of its anhydrous chloride or fluoride with metallic calcium. It's estimated
abundance in the earth's crust is 1.3 mg slash kg. HOMEM obeys the Odo-Harkins rule, as a
non-numbered element. It is less abundant than its immediate even numbered neighbors,
disproseium and herbium. However, it is the most abundant of the odd numbered heavy lanthanides.
The principal current source are some of the ion-ed sorption clays of southern China.
Some of these have a rare earth composition similar to that found in senotime or gadolinite
dotatrium makes up about 2 thirds of the total by mass, HOMEM is around 1.5%. The original
ors themselves are very lean, maybe only 0.1% total lanthanide, but are easily extracted. HOMEM
is relatively inexpensive for a rare earth metal with the price about used 1000 slash kg.
HOMEM has the highest magnetic strength of any element, and therefore is used to create the
strongest artificially generated magnetic fields, when placed within high strength magnets as a
magnetic pole piece, also called a magnetic flux concentrator. Since it can absorb nuclear
fish and bread neutrons, it is also used as a burnable poison to regulate nuclear reactors.
HOMEM is used in itrium iron garnet, YIG, and itrium lanthanum fluoride, YLF, solid-state
lasers found in microwave equipment, which are in turn found in a variety of medical and dental
settings. HOMEM lasers emit a 2.1 micrometers. They are used in medical, dental, and fiber optical
applications. HOMEM is one of the colorants used for cubics or conia and glass, providing yellow
or red coloring. Glass containing HOMEM oxide and HOMEM oxide solutions usually in perchloric acid,
have sharp optical absorption peaks in the spectral range 200 to 900 nanometers. They are
therefore used as a calibration standard for optical spectrophotometers and are available commercially.
The radioactive but long-lived HOMEM, C-Iced hopes above, is used in calibration of gamma-ray
spectrometers. In March 2017, IBM announced that they have developed a technique to store one
bit of data on a single HOMEM atom set on a bit of magnesium oxide. And HOMEM plays no biological
role in humans, but its salts are able to stimulate metabolism. Humans typically consume about
a milligram of HOMEM a year.plants do not readily take up HOMEM from the soil. Some vegetables have
had their HOMEM content measured, and it amounted to 100 parts per trillion. Large amounts of HOMEM salts
can cause severe damage if inhaled, consumed orally, or injected. The biological effects of HOMEM over
a long period of time are not known. HOMEM has a low level of acute toxicity.

Holmium

Holmium is a chemical element with symbol Ho and atomic number 67. Part of the lanthanide series, holmium is a rare-earth element. Holmium was discovered by Swedish chemist Per Theodor Cleve. Its oxide was first isolated from rare-earth ores in 1878. The element's name comes from "Holmia", the Latin name for the city of Stockholm.

Elemental holmium is a relatively soft and malleable silvery-white metal. It is too reactive to be found uncombined in nature, but when isolated, is relatively stable in dry air at room temperature. However, it reacts with water and corrodes readily and also burns in air when heated.

Holmium is found in the minerals monazite and gadolinite and is usually commercially extracted from monazite using ion-exchange techniques. Its compounds in nature and in nearly all of its laboratory chemistry are trivalently oxidized, containing Ho(III) ions. Trivalent holmium ions have fluorescent properties similar to many other rare-earth ions (while yielding their own set of unique emission light lines), and thus are used in the same way as some other rare earths in certain laser and glass-colorant applications.

Holmium has the highest magnetic permeability of any element and therefore is used for the polepieces of the strongest static magnets. Because holmium strongly absorbs neutrons, it is also used as a burnable poison in nuclear reactors.

Holmium is a relatively soft and malleable element that is fairly corrosion-resistant and stable in dry air at standard temperature and pressure. In moist air and at higher temperatures, however, it quickly oxidizes, forming a yellowish oxide. In pure form, holmium possesses a metallic, bright silvery luster.
